articles.title: Built from Scratch: How a meteorologist built a better umbrella
articles.summary: Rick Reichmuth, after 19 years as a Fox meteorologist, turned his sights on creating the perfect umbrella. Now, Weatherman sells five categories of umbrellas, ponchos, hats and more.
articles.body: Rick Reichmuth didn’t set out to start a business. He just wanted a better umbrella. After 19 years as a Fox meteorologist, he knew how to predict the weather, yet he still couldn't find an umbrella that could survive it. Staring at racks of umbrellas on the streets of New York City, he was struck by a glaring gap in the market: While categories like bandages and tissues had iconic, trusted household names, buying an umbrella was a total gamble. CEO SUNDAY: ARMY VETERAN TURNED HEALTH TECH BOSS CALLS SUPPORT FOR THOSE WHO SERVED A ‘SACRED OBLIGATION’ After searching for a standout umbrella brand and coming up empty, he asked himself, "Why not create my own?" Nobody knows the elements better than a meteorologist, and with that, Weatherman was born. Stepping out into the rain Reichmuth started by taking apart hundreds of umbrellas in his New York City apartment. His goal was simple: He wanted to reverse-engineer how they worked, pinpoint why they failed and establish the blueprint for a truly great umbrella. Armed with that research, he teamed up with an industrial designer friend to build a model that was strong, durable and built to withstand the elements. CEO SUNDAY: AVELO AIRLINES CEO REVEALS THE HABIT HE CREDITS FOR HIS SUCCESS Yet, despite a lengthy career in meteorology, nothing had prepared him for the ins and outs of running a business. Reichmuth remembers looking at the very first Weatherman prototype and thinking, "Wow, I think the hard part is finally over." As it turned out, the work was just beginning. Weathering the storm Running a small business tested Reichmuth in ways forecasting never did. He said it was a journey marked by steep trials and hard-earned lessons that he still calls the hardest thing he's ever done. When Weatherman debuted in 2017, the lineup consisted of just two designs: a collapsible model and a stick umbrella. BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A RENTED KITCHEN AND HAND-SQUEEZED FRUIT BECAME A VERSATILE MIXER Both have since been retired, a testament to how relentlessly the brand has refined and upgraded its engineering over the last nine years. Entering a new industry without a product development background was intimidating, and early missteps hit hard. "Early on, a failure or setback could really knock me down," Reichmuth admits. "Sometimes I'd spend weeks feeling stuck, second-guessing decisions or worrying about what went wrong. That paralysis often became a bigger problem than the original mistake." "Admitting what you don't know is actually one of the most valuable things you can do." Over time, learning to absorb those blows became Weatherman's greatest catalyst for growth. Today, Reichmuth caps his frustration at a few hours before pivoting back to problem-solving. "Admitting what you don't know is actually one of the most valuable things you can do," he says. "Once you accept that failure is normal — not something to be ashamed of — it becomes a whole lot easier to keep moving forward." The sun comes out The ultimate validation didn't come from TV ratings; it came on the crowded sidewalks of New York. "I'd be walking around and suddenly see someone carrying one of our umbrellas," Reichmuth says. "That never gets old." BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION The sweetest moments, however, are the ones where customers praise the gear without any idea who he is. "They hadn't bought it because they'd seen me on television," he points out. "They bought it because a friend recommended it, or they discovered it online, or they'd heard it was a great umbrella." For an entrepreneur who started by tearing apart umbrellas in his apartment, earning that pure, organic trust was everything. Today, with Weatherman expanding and solidly profitable over the last few years, the journey has more than paid off. Staying dry What separates Weatherman from the sea of disposable umbrellas? Engineering. Armed with heavy-duty fiberglass frames and water-repellent recycled fabric, the canopies are wind-tunnel tested to withstand gusts of up to 55 mph. They double as sun protection with built-in UPF 50+, and feature smooth auto-open mechanisms to spare users the classic rain-soaked struggle. CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS But the true differentiator is how Weatherman approaches design: by use case. Recognizing that a city commuter has different needs than a backcountry hiker or a weekend golfer, the brand organizes its lineup into distinct categories like Walk, Trek, Travel, Golf and Kids — outfitting each with specialized features like reflective trim or pocket-friendly sizing to match real-world habits. Rainbow on the horizon Today, Weatherman has expanded into sun shirts and ponchos for adults, kids and even pets — designed for real-life moments like youth soccer games or unexpected vacation downpours. Recognizing that not everyone wants to splurge on rain gear they hope to rarely use, Reichmuth and his team are developing a more affordable sister brand. Set to debut in 2027, it will bring Weatherman's signature thoughtful engineering to a wider, budget-conscious audience. Still, one thing is for sure: Forecasts aren’t always certain, but Reichmuth’s goal is to help people stay prepared when conditions take an unexpected turn. Shop Weatherman Pick the right umbrella for you, whether you're hiking, hitting the golf course or just walking to work. articles.title: Insiders Reveal 49ers’ Asking Price to Vikings for Mac Jones
articles.summary: The Minnesota Vikings were looking everywhere for a QB leading up to the 4 pm Nov. 10 trade deadline. Eventually, they were able to trade a 2027 third-round...
articles.body:
The Minnesota Vikings were looking everywhere for a QB leading up to the 4 pm Nov. 10 trade deadline. Eventually, they were able to trade a 2027 third-round pick to the Las Vegas Raiders for Kirk Cousins.

Nonetheless, the Vikings were looking at every option to find a QB who could get their offense trending in the right direction midway through the season. One of the names that Minnesota called about was the San Francisco 49ers' Mac Jones.

On Nov. 14, ESPN NFL insiders Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport reported what the Niners were demanding from the Vikings to trade Jones to a potential NFC opponent in the playoffs.

"When the Vikings called San Francisco as part of due diligence in their search for a quarterback, sources told ESPN that Niners general manager John Lynch informed Minnesota brass that it would take a second-round pick and more for Jones," the insiders wrote in their report.

"Perhaps a second-rounder and a middle-round pick might have gotten a trade done. Instead, because of the high cost associated with the veteran quarterback, the conversations ended there and Jones remains a valued member of the 49ers."

The Niners likely view Jones as an important insurance policy should Brock Purdy get hurt, as last season he showed that he can steady the ship if an injury does happen. Jones has a passer rating of 97.4 with 2,151 yards, 13 touchdowns, and six interceptions in 13 games for the 49ers, per StatMuse .

Kirk Cousins' Transition Back to Vikings Offense Going Well

Meanwhile, ESPN NFL senior reporter Jeremy Fowler shared an update on Cousins' transition back into the Vikings offense after being away for three years.

"It was as smooth as can be," Fowler said during a Nov. 14 appearance on "SportsCenter." "Remember, he's got six teammates in the starting offensive line depth chart right now that it's sort of too familiar for him. But the first thing he did, I was told, when he got there was get with his center, Blake Brandel, to just get through the snaps and make sure they have the same cadence on the play action under center. We got to work on that. They feel like he's throwing the ball well.

"Kevin O'Connell's added some wrinkles in his offense throughout the years since Cousins has been there, but it remains mostly intact. So they feel like it's been as good as it could have gone for a short three-day window for him to literally come into town on a Wednesday, prep for three days, and be the starter."

KOC Isn't Looking to Overwhelm Kirk Cousins

Nonetheless, while Cousins' transition back into the Vikings' offense has reportedly been smooth, head coach Kevin O'Connell isn't looking to overwhelm the veteran as he shared an update on how they are getting the veteran QB comfortable for the Week 10 game against the Green Bay Packers .

"He believes wholeheartedly in what we do and his role in moving the team," O'Connell told reporters on Nov. 13 . "So really, it's about getting the plan working with him and getting him the plan in real time, in many ways, play by play, situation by situation, and then letting him digest it and getting back together and talking through things post-install, post-reps in practice.

"We'll spend some time together [on Nov. 13] and use every moment we have up until the game. But I'm really looking forward to seeing him play. Though it's something we've always known about him, the way he threw the football this week was a really cool thing to see."

articles.title: Despite Praise, Shifty WR Must Wait to Make Steelers Debut
articles.summary: Max Hurleman‘s name popped up as one to watch this week as the Pittsburgh Steelers prepared for Sunday night’s AFC […]
articles.body:
Max Hurleman 's name popped up as one to watch this week as the Pittsburgh Steelers prepared for Sunday night's AFC North road matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Despite the votes of confidence from Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers, the second-year receiver won't be making his NFL debut just yet.

"I mean, how do you not love Max (Hurelman)? McCarthy said Thursday. "I mean, Max is, he's one of the guys you, as a new coach, new coaching staff. You come in here every day doing everything right. GPS was, [he] burned it up. I mean, just, the guy has an incredible workload capacity, work ethic, so unfortunate that he got hurt when he did. I felt that he truly performed to a level that he deserved a 53-man roster spot. So, it'll be great to get him back and get him back into the fold."

Hurleman played collegiately at Colgate before transferring to Notre Dame. He stuck with the Steelers after a rookie minicamp tryout, then spent the entirety of his rookie season on the practice squad without being elevated.

Hurleman had three receptions for 46 yards in the Steelers' 28-9 preseason win over the Green Bay Packers.

articles.title: Bryson DeChambeau Builds His Legacy Back Home In Clovis
articles.summary: Bryson DeChambeau unveils an 18-hole course and homes in Clovis, California. The two-time major champ reinvests his LIV earnings into his hometown roots.
articles.body:
Bryson DeChambeau is building an 18-hole golf course and a residential community right in his hometown of Clovis, California, according to Billionaires.Africa . The two-time U.S. Open champion announced this massive project on Friday, November 13. He plans to turn the historic McFarlane Ranch into a hub for golf and living.

The project covers about 200 acres on the northeastern edge of Fresno. DeChambeau expects the city to approve the plan within 18 months. He told reporters that a significant portion of his LIV Golf earnings is being allocated to finance this development. His contract with the Saudi-backed league was widely reported at about $125 million when he joined in 2022. That financial backing allows him to reshape his local landscape without waiting for outside investors.

Most golf stars chase fame in big cities like Los Angeles or Miami. DeChambeau is doing the opposite by investing in a city of about 120,000 people. He grew up in Clovis and attended Clovis East High School before turning pro. The plan pairs the new golf course with homes for people to buy. It creates a long-term legacy rather than a quick profit flip.

With five LIV Golf titles to his name, DeChambeau has secured nine victories during his PGA Tour career. He also has two major championships to his name. His scientific approach to the game made him one of the most talked-about players ever. Now he is applying that same focus to building a community. His academic path included studying physics at Southern Methodist University, where he claimed the 2015 NCAA individual title. That same drive for precision is now being used to design a course and a neighborhood.

On his YouTube channel, DeChambeau boasts a subscriber count exceeding three million. His fame in content creation matches the renown he has achieved through his competitive career. While other players focus on social media clips, he is building something you can walk on. The Head Professional at Sugarloaf Golf Club, Oscar Parks, said DeChambeau is very down to earth. Parks noted that the group did not have a ton of lists or demands during their time together.

"They were very professional and they didn't waste a lot of time," Parks explained in an interview. He further noted that the group consisted entirely of ordinary guys. This attitude fits the Clovis project perfectly. DeChambeau does not need a fancy clubhouse to prove his worth. He needs a place where he can play and build with people he knows.

articles.title: Packers Get Encouraging Update on RB’s Injury as Return Timeline Emerges
articles.summary: Riding 6-3 momentum after a dominant 45-27 win over the New England Patriots, the Green Bay Packers enter a crucial Week 10 NFC North clash against the Minne...
articles.body:
Riding 6-3 momentum after a dominant 45-27 win over the New England Patriots, the Green Bay Packers enter a crucial Week 10 NFC North clash against the Minnesota Vikings with a major question mark in their backfield.

But last Sunday, Josh Jacobs broke his right ring finger in the first quarter. While the star back has already been ruled out ahead of Green Bay's Week 11 bye, the team just received an encouraging update regarding how long he will actually be sidelined.

Josh Jacobs' finger surgery update and recovery timeline

Jacobs injured his hand while trying to stiff-arm Patriots defensive back Craig Woodson near the sideline in the first quarter, finishing with just four carries for five yards and a fumble before heading to the locker room.

Having played just three games this season after missing the first six on the Commissioner's Exempt List, the veteran running back leaves a noticeable void in Matt LaFleur's offense.

Earlier in the week, NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported that Jacobs could return in as little as two to three weeks following the procedure. On Saturday, Tom Pelissero confirmed that Jacobs underwent successful surgery on Friday, Nov. 13, in Los Angeles and "should be back in the next few weeks."

Because an injured reserve stint requires a mandatory four-game absence, Green Bay opted against placing Jacobs on IR ahead of Sunday's matchup. Since the Week 11 bye gives him extra recovery time without missing another game, he has a chance to return as early as Week 12 against the Los Angeles Rams on Thanksgiving Eve or Week 13 against the New Orleans Saints.

With the three-time Pro Bowler sidelined, second-year running back Kaleb Johnson is the top candidate to lead Green Bay's backfield against Minnesota. After Jacobs exited in Week 9, Johnson delivered the Packers' best rushing performance of the season with 14 carries for 68 yards and a touchdown.

The Athletic's Matt Schneidman also noted that Green Bay should depend heavily on Johnson over MarShawn Lloyd. Alongside Lloyd, Pierre Strong Jr. and Chris Brooks are also available on the roster, giving LaFleur multiple options to keep the offense balanced while Jacobs recovers through the bye.

articles.body:
The final round of the 2026 Austin Championship has been moved up due to inclement weather expected on Sunday.

Golf Channel's will start its Round 4 coverage at 12:30 p.m. ET with a half-hour Golf Central Pregame airing before.

The final round tee times at Fazio Canyons will be posted at the conclusion of Round 3 play on Saturday.

Currently the leaderboard is crowded at the inaugural tournament with Trace Crowe, Ben Kohles and Chad Ramey in contention on Moving Day.

articles.title: 3 things on Packers defense vs. Vikings: Cisse vs. Jefferson Part 2
articles.summary: Brandon Cisse gets a chance to show his growth in his second matchup with Justin Jefferson after a 'welcome to the NFL' moment back in Week 1.
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers defense is looking for redemption after giving up 39 points to Minnesota back in Week 1, and they will now face a new quarterback at Lambeau Field on Sunday after the Vikings traded for old friend Kirk Cousins.

Many of the points surrendered in the season opener came off turnovers which put Minnesota in the red zone, and one touchdown drive was heavily aided by some baffling officiating Jonathan Gannon's unit will want to show that what happened in Week 1 was a fluke.

Here are three thoughts on the matchup between the Packers defense and the Vikings offense.

Cousins will elevate the Vikings offense

Minnesota had to do something at quarterback with the uninspiring combination of Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz threatening to waste an elite defense as the offense ranked 28th in expected points added (EPA) per pass and 29th in passing success rate.

Kirk Cousins should be a legitimate upgrade over the previous options. His numbers are not gaudy, but he was playing good ball for a Raiders offense lacking talent, ranking 11th in EPA per pass and 8th in success rate. He is in the top half of the league in a lot of different metrics.

The Vikings' offensive line is solid, allowing the 9th lowest pressure rate in the league, and Cousins should accentuate that, as he does a great job of getting the ball out, ranking 2nd in pressure-to-sack rate. That will be a big difference from Murray and Wentz, who rank 34th and 40th.

Green Bay will be hoping to catch Cousins at a good time as he may take some time getting back up to speed in Kevin O'Connell's defense having only arrived in Minnesota on Tuesday, but there is no doubt his presence makes this a tougher game than it would have been.

Minnesota cannot run the ball, ranking 29th in both EPA/rush and rushing success rate. They will also be without T.J. Hockenson and Jauan Jennings this week, while Jordan Addison is questionable with a thumb injury.

But Cousins will have Justin Jefferson at his disposal, and that might be all he needs. The Packers secondary held Jefferson in check for much of the Week 1 contest, but he got them eventually, putting up a season-high 92 yards and two touchdowns.

That included a 39-yard score against Brandon Cisse who was making his pro debut. It was a 'welcome to the NFL' moment for Cisse, who has gone from strength to strength throughout his rookie season since then, allowing only one more touchdown which came back in Week 2.

Green Bay's corners will need to bring their A-game on Sunday, and the matchup with Jefferson provides Cisse with another opportunity to show what he has learned in the two months since they last met.

The Packers are pretty banged up on defense right now. They will of course be without Edgerrin Cooper and Javon Hargrave who started the Week 1 game against the Vikings, and the status of several other key defenders is up in the air ahead of Sunday's game.

Xavier McKinney popped up on the injury report as a limited practice participant with a foot issue on Friday.

Losing one of the safeties who have been so key to Gannon's defense could be a big problem, and while Javon Bullard told reporters he will play, he is questionable with ankle and knee injuries after only practicing once this week, in a limited capacity on Friday.

Green Bay's pass rush has been effective even without Micah Parsons, albeit aided by Gannon's creativity. Not having Lukas Van Ness – who like Bullard only practiced on Friday and was limited with a back problem – would be a blow as he has been their best edge defender this season.

Elsewhere, it seems Zaire Franklin is one again unlikely to play due to his shin injury, listed as doubtful.

Gannon's group has managed to not really skip a beat despite some key injuries throughout the year so far, but if all of those players are not available against Minnesota, it could have an adverse effect on their ability to hold the Vikings offense down.

articles.title: Golfer Tim O'Neal talks PGA diversity at Phoenix Charles Schwab Cup
articles.summary: Pro golfer Tim O'Neal spoke to The Arizona Republic about his late mom inspiring his career comeback and financing for Black golfers.
articles.body:
Tim O'Neal had a calm smile during his practice shots at the Phoenix Country Club. Clad in his crisp blue long-sleeve shirt and Servpro badge, white hat and matching shorts, O'Neal was in the Valley competing in his third straight Charles Schwab Cup Championship, Nov. 12-15.

O'Neal was among 36 qualifiers for the PGA Tour Champions season finale. He is the lone African-American competing for his first title.

"Hopefully, other golfers of color will realize and see if I can do it, they can do it too," O'Neal told The Arizona Republic earlier this week.

O'Neal is approaching nearly 30 years as a pro and fourth PGA Tour Champions season. He started on the Korn Ferry Tour as a rookie in 1997 out of Jackson State University, a rarity for a player from a historically Black college or university (HBCU). That was the same year Tiger Woods turned pro and became the first African-American to win the Masters.

Since then, golf diversity has reached an all-time high of 25%, or seven million, among Black, Asian, or Latinx players in 2024, up from 8% in 1990, per the National Golf Foundation (NGF) and United States Golf Association (USGA).

Black pro golfers also on the current tour include Harold Varner II, Joseph Bramlett and Cameron Champ.

"With Tiger getting on tour, winning majors and dominating for a long time, that definitely I would think has had an effect," O'Neal said.

O'Neal, 52, has had a strong 2026, with five top-10 finishes through 27 events. And he's still riding the coattails of his sole career victory at the Dominion Energy Charity Classic in October 2024.

See final round of 2026 WM Phoenix Open in photos

That's a turnaround from the multiple heartbreaks at qualifying school (Q-school) earlier in his career. He missed earning his PGA Tour card twice by one stroke in 2001 and 2004, before finally securing it in 2008.

"You get a little smarter, course management's a little bit better," O'Neal said. "Probably in my younger days probably a little more aggressive on the course. I'm now a bit more conservative. ... But once I got on the Champions Tour, I think for me I still need some more work, but short game was the main thing. I've improved there but I still have some room to grow there as well and just getting more comfortable with these guys out here, some of the best players in the world."

O'Neal was sponsored by actor and hip hop legend Will Smith earlier in his career. The loss of his PGA card, Nationwide Tour privileges and lack of money nearly caused O'Neal to quit for good.

From 2010-11, O'Neal worked and gave lessons at Edwin Watts golf shop in his native Savannah, Georgia, while he played in mini tournaments over the next two years. His late mother Eva O'Neal, who passed away in 2020, urged him to stick with the game that she and his dad taught him to play.

In 2013, O'Neal played in the eGOLF Tour in Charlotte, which helped jump-start his career. He then went to Morocco in the Moroccan Golf Federation and played six tournaments and earned $7,500 in each of his three wins. He continued to fund his own comeback as that prize money got him into another bigger European tournament, Trophy Hassan II, and he won $18,000 by finishing in the top 20.

Then got into Q-school at the PGA Tour Latinoamérica in South America in 2013. Then, in 2014, he played again on the Korn Ferry tour.

"Twenty-something years ago, you could probably skimp here and skimp there to find a way to get through, but now it's impossible," O'Neal told The Arizona Republic. "Everyone's good, everyone has the best coaches and best courses to play, and it's sad to say this but if you don't have financial backing, you really don't have a chance. And it costs about $100,000 a year to really do it the right way."

Many Black amateur golfers face the same issue to develop and become pros, especially those from HBCUs.

Jackson State put a two-year suspension on its men's and women's golf program as part of the university's $106 million budget cuts, that included travel spending, in 2017. After a protracted hiatus, which O'Neal called "sad" for the former "powerhouse in golf," Jackson State resumed its program in 2025.

In addition, there are PGA events and programs such as the APGA Tour , Pathway To Progression and Coca-Cola partnership with the PGA Tour for the HBCU Golf Impact Grant, which pledges $250,000 to 10 partner schools and 16 golf programs.

Lucrative college NIL deals and allocation mostly goes to more popular college sports such as basketball and football.

"If it wasn't for the people who helped me along the way to get here now, unless you come from a wealthy family, very expensive sport to play with equipment and all the stuff you need to really make it,'' O'Neal said. "These financial groups, whatever they can do to help golfers get to the next level, you need it because there's very few golfers who made it that didn't have backing behind them."
